For this reason, I prefer the metaphor of the ambient. What is ambient is immersive, osmotic, peripheral. Ambience is not so link driven, for it suggests many tactile forms besides connections among already established points or nodes. The link gives us little leeway with the more ephemeral, nuratic modalities of everyday life. Indeed, the network is ultimately still invested in binaries (movement and node, line and point), even if such binaries are wrenched by the strange loops of emergent behavior. The richly osmotic character of ambience includes choric engagement and interaction beyond the link. As I will address in the next chapter, this includes affect: affect certainly circulates in and gives rise to networks, but we need to augment this understanding of affect as more fundamental, being the mood, or affective comportment, from which our attitudes, decisions, and actions emerge. The attunement to what is choric reminds us that we cannot reduce the world to simple presence, to what is already revealed. but must rather attend to genesis, how things come to be as they are. The concept of ambience is better suited to gathering kairos and logos into a worldliness that includes but also transcends the human, showing how they take part in us even as they will us, speak us.

But how, exactly, do kairos and logos pick out various ways in which discourse and environs come to speak or will us? What can show this to be something other than a return to the subject/object split, which privileges

an objective, exterior environment over a subject? As I have previously argued. subject and object derive from an originary belongingness, and if we want to keep these terms, we need to see them more as a "mutual taking part in." But insofar as this "taking part in" is ultimately ambient, it simultaneously includes and exceeds the "subject"; only in this sense can we understand the kairotic environs as willing us. Nor, as should become clear, am I merely collapsing distinct realms into an abstract unity; this is equally impossible, for the ambient, if thought alongside complexity theory, can be seen as an emergent level of order discontinuous from what is given by the ensemble of original individual elements. Rather than possess some a priori ontological status, distinctions emerge dynamically and fluidly within the situation and are ultimately only an additional modality in the overall ambience. As I began this chapter with Taylor's meditation on a writer writing, I want to once again consider what happens as a writer writes. But I begin doing so by going back before Taylor.

Barrett J. Mandel's 1980 essay "The Writer Writing Is Not at Home" stands as remarkably prescient for my purposes, and it makes an illuminating contrast with Taylor's work. Mandel opens his essay with a snippet from an interview with the American painter Jasper Johns, conducted, oddly enough, by Michael Crichton:

The author [Crichton] asks Johns why he has just made a change in the handle of a spoon in a lithograph on which he is working. Johns answers, "Because I did." The author asks, "But what did you see?" Johns: '·I saw that it should be changed." Author: "Well, if you changed it, what was wrong with it before?" Johns: "Nothing. I tend to think one thing is as good as another." Author: "Then why change it?" Johns, after a sigh and a pause: "Well, I may change it again." Author: "Why?" Johns: "Well, I won't know until I doit." (370)

This is high comedy, no doubt, with Crichton coming off as a clueless interviewer. 19 Still, Mandel notes the difficulties in communication and defends Johns as being as honest as he can. The artist, Mandel argues, creates "out ofno prior knowledge, thought, plan, or expectations" (370). Plans and thoughts do come into play, but "the work of art does not arise from them; they do not cause the work of art to materialize" (370). Ann Berthoff makes a similar point when she snipes about a grad student who writes something down, erases, writes again, erases, and never gets past the blank sheet. 20

Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

So far I have been arguing that dwelling and the fourfold grant insight into an originary affectability materialized in things and in the world's worlding. As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. Here are ambiguities of substance. In being identified with B, A is “substantially one” with a person other than himself. Yet at the same time he remains unique, an individual locus of motives. Thus he is both joined and separate, at once a distinct substance and substantial with another. While consubstandal with its parents, with the “firsts” from which it is derived, the offspring is nonetheless apart from them. In this sense, there is nothing abstruse in the statement that the offspring both is and is not one with its parentage. Similarly, two persons may be identified in terms of some principle they share in common, an “identi­ fication” that does not deny their distinctness. To identify A with B is to make A “consubstandal” with B. Accord­ ingly, since our Grammar of Motives was constructed about “sub­ stance” as key term, the related rhetoric selects its nearest equivalent in the areas of persuasion and dissuasion, communicadon and polemic. And our third volume, Symbolic of Motives, should be built about identity as dtular or ancestral term, the “first” to which all other terms could be reduced and from which they could then be derived or gen­ erated, as from a common spirit. The thing’s identity would here be its uniqueness as an entity in itself and by itself, a demarcated unit having its own pardcular structure. However, “substance” is an abstruse philosophic term, beset by a long history of quandaries and puzzlements. It names so paradoxical a function in men’s systematic terminologies, that thinkers finally tried to abolish it altogether—and in recent years they have often persuaded themselves that they really did abolish it from their terminologies of modves. They abolished the term, but it is doubtful whether they can ever abolish the function of that term, or even whether they should want to. A doctrine of consubstantiality, either explicit or implicit, may be necessary to any way of life. For substance, in the old philoso­ phies, was an act; and a way of life is an acting-together; and in act­ ing together, men have common sensations, concepts, images, ideas, attitudes that make them consubstantied. The Grammar dealt with the universal paradoxes of substance. It considered resources of placement and definition common to all thought. The Symbolic should deal with unique individuals, each its own peculiarly constructed act, or form. These unique “constitu­ tions” being capable of treatment in isolation, the Symbolic should

universe

THE RANGE OF RHETORIC consider them primarily in their capacity as singulars, each a separate of discourse (though there are also respects in which they are consubstantial with others of their kind, since they can be classed with other unique individuals as joint participants in common principles,

or en-

possessors of the same or similar properties). The Rhetoric deals with the possibilities of classification in its par­ tisan aspects; it considers the ways in which individuals are at odds with one another, or become identified with groups more or less at odds with one another. Why “at odds," you may ask, when the titular term is “identifica­ tion”? Because, to begin with “identification” is, by the same token, though roundabout, to confront the implications of division. And so, in the end, men are brought to that most tragically ironic of all divi­ sions, or conflicts, wherein millions of cooperative acts go into the preparation for one single destructive act. We refer to that ultimate disease of cooperation: war. (You will understand war much better if you think of it, not simply as strife come to a head, but rather as a disease, or perversion of communion. Modern war characteristically requires a myriad of constructive acts for each destructive one; before each culminating blast there must be a vast network of interlocking operations, directed communally.) Identification is affirmed with earnestness precisely because there is division. Identification is compensatory to division. If men were nor apart from one another, there would be no need for the rhetorician to proclaim their unity. If men were wholly and truly of one sub­ stance, absolute communication would be of man’s very essence. It would not be an ideal, as it now is, partly embodied in material condi­ tions and partly frustrated by these same conditions; rather, it would be as natural, spontaneous, and total as with those ideal prototypes of communication, the theologian’s angels, or “messengers.” The Grammar was at peace insofar as it contemplated the paradoxes common to all men, the universal resources of verbal placement. The Symbolic should be at peace, in that the individual substances, tides, or constituted acts are there considered in their uniqueness, hence outside the realm of conflict. In all such partly verbal, partly nonverbal kinds of rhetorical devices, the nonverbal element also persuades by reason of its symbolic character. Paper need not know the meaning of fire in order to burn. But in the "idea" offire there is a persuasive ingredient. By this route something of the rhetorical motive comes to lurk in every "meaning" however purely "scientific" its pretensions. Wherever there is persuasion, there is rhetoric. And wherever there is "meaning," there is "persuasion." Food, eaten and digested, is not rhetorical. But in the meaning o[food there is much rhetoric, the meaning being persuasive enough for the idea of food to be used, like the ideas ofreligion, as a rhetorical device of statesmen. (RM 172-73)

This passage seems far from clear. Additionally, the numerous ironizing quotation marks and italics indicate various forms of pressure and stress. The word meaning, not insignificantly, is italicized twice and twice placed in quotation marks. What does meaning mean here? The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. Meaning is gleaned from the symbolicity that drapes over (or maybe permeates) the mundane world, circulating it as the significance available to us. The mention of science is important here, for Burke is clearly dissatisfied with a positivist, scientific claim of mere facticity for things of the world, as if measuring qualia sufficed for generating meaning. Thus, he will grant that paper, being paper, has no ideas as such; its rapid oxidation at temperatures around 451 degrees Fahrenheit is a purely chemical reaction. But to remain at this level is to willfully (or methodologically) remain at observation degree zero, and it obscures fire's role in human affairs. When Bradbury's Fireman comes to

burn the books, though, we move into a different realm, one of meaning, and we see that fire is a full rhetorical participant. Fire, then, is more than just a sensed material phenomenon; its integration into the human world necessitates ideas. These ideas mean, and insofar as they mean, they bodily invoke, and insofar as they bodily invoke, they persuade.

As I observed in my discussion of Hawhee, this is not an abstract notion of fire as meaningful; rather, it is one entirely grounded in the bodily integration of ideas stemming from physical experience. As Burke puts it in Attitudes toward History, "our primeval ancestors, by learning language, no longer experienced a sensation solely as a sensation" (382). As he goes on to explain, we may like the warmth ofa fire, and such warmth is certainly a sensation, but as soon as we start putting such experience into language, the words come to "tell a story"; as a result, attitudes (or affective stances) can emerge and be deployed across various forms of discursive interaction, such as the movement from "that feels warm" to the observation that someone is "warm-hearted" (Burke,AH383).

This elevation of meaning over mundane, objective matter is further evinced in other passages. Later in A Rhetoric of Motives Burke again discusses the effect of material phenomena. This time he calls them a form of intuition, and he then tethers intuition to a notion of infancy. One can perceive a seashell, for instance, and note the generative regularity of its spiral. but without more firmly and robustly grasping the intelligibility of that spiral in the world of human meaning, such as reasoning out the mathematical functions that generate various spirals, such an encounter remains stuck in what he terms "infancy," a notion he further compares to the "realm of the unconscious in dreams" (RM 174-75). But before we begin complaining about the terribly slanted and problematic valuation here, where conscious reason trumps infantile intuition, we must see the antistrophe he proposes immediately thereafter. If a poem brings up springtime, Burke explains, we must understand the locution beyond the "positivist's 'fact'" of spring (175). Burke's explanation for this is quote worthy:

An "intuition" of spring is not a mere passive perception, a datum of sensory (or even supersensory) knowledge. My arguments for the importance of ambience should not be understood as any simple call to "pay attention." One is in any event only partially aware of ongoing events within one's environs at any given time. The environs are ready-to-hand, yes, but they now have agentive powers Heidegger's hammer never had. Emile A arts and Stefano Marzano point out, "As technology becomes hidden within these static, unintelligent objects, they will become subjects, active and intelligent actors in our environment ... [and the] immaterial world of our interactions with them-services, games, entertainment, information, communication-will become more prominent in our lives" (8-9). Greenfield argues that ubiquitous computing "will disturb unwritten agreements about workspace and homespace, the presentation of self and the right to privacy. It contains an inherent, unsettling potential for panoptical surveillance, regulation, and 'rationalization.' Its presence in our lives will transfigure our notions of space and time, self and other, citizen and society in ways we haven't begun to contemplate" (3). In short, ambient intelligence radically changes who we are in our environs; it

situates us differently in the world, evoking other ways of being. It thereby also reveals rhetoric to us differently than it has appeared heretofore. Ambience thus teaches us that we cannot rely solely on salience, attention, and consciousness to guide us.

Rhetoric has much to learn from music on this score. I am claiming that ambient music is an important development, both in its own right as a form of thinking (and not simply as expression ofhuman thought and affect) and as something that shows how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to the music's creation but to what we take the music to be. Music is not just the salience of its affective work. Ambient music has still other rhetorical dimensions, including politics. It has ramifications for how we dwell in the world. Eno claims that ambient music is directly political: "The decision to stop seeing yourself as the centre of the world, to see yourself as part of the greater flow of things, as having limited options and responsibility for your actions[.] ... that is political theory: and it's where the music grows from" (qtd. in Tamm 91).

It is hardly a stretch to see that these political insights resonate with the extension of digital computing into things and environs. As Eno is quite aware, there are both opportunities and dangers here, which is why transforming how one sees oneself in the world is integral to a politics attuned to these dangers. 21 So, much as ambient music does, ubiquitous computing (ambient intelligence) showcases how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to our everyday activity but to a conception of dynamic life itself. We need not overstate the case by claiming we are on the threshold of a brave new world. Rather, we are simply seeing capacities, implications, and energies as previously assembled now giving way to vibrant and different intensities and assemblages. But we cannot ignore how these different forms also assemble new forms oflife, or new ways of being-in-the-world.

Rhetoric, Ambience, Dwelling

We need conceptions ofrhetoric that keep pace with these transformations and their attendant opportunities and dangers, that not only help us make sense of them but enable us to flourish (and that will, of course, spur new transformations). We do not need a new rhetoric, however; rather, we must work anew with what has been brought forward in rhetorical theory and practice.
